item.content:encoded:
Gov.-elect Tony Ada and Lt. Gov.-elect E.J. Calvo said their incoming administration will open cabinet and senior staff positions to public applicants, with an emphasis on professional experience, qualifications, and commitment to public service rather than political affiliation.

During their first press conference as governor and lieutenant governor-elect, the two outlined plans to establish an online application portal where interested residents, including current government employees, can submit resumes and apply for positions within the incoming administration.

Jadeen Perez, who will chair the transition team’s Committee on Administration and Appointees, said the committee plans to begin accepting applications after the election results are certified on Nov. 19.

Applicants will undergo background checks and an evaluation of their qualifications before the committee submits recommendations to Ada and Calvo.

Ada said the application process will be open to anyone interested in serving, including members of the current administration.

“The bottom line is, everybody working together, regardless of party affiliation,” Ada said. “Election is over. Now it’s time for everybody to come together and work together.”

The incoming administration has also established three principal transition committees to guide the transfer of government responsibilities. The Committee on Government Operations and Efficiency, chaired by Nate Denight, will review the operations of government agencies, identify opportunities to improve efficiency, and assess existing challenges. The Committee on Administration and Appointees will oversee the recruitment and evaluation of potential cabinet members and senior staff, while the Committee on Inaugural Arrangements, chaired by Piti Mayor Jesse Alig, will coordinate inauguration preparations.

Denight said the government operations committee will establish additional subcommittees to review the island’s 52 government agencies. The committees will meet with agency management and staff to identify what is working, what needs improvement, and what resources may be needed.

Their findings will be compiled into a final transition report outlining each department’s current situation, objectives, and recommendations. Transition chair Jerry Crisostomo said the report will help Ada and Calvo determine their administration’s priorities and guide appointments ahead of their expected Jan. 4 start in office.

Ada said the incoming administration will first focus on completing a smooth transition and assessing the government’s financial position and operational needs before determining its immediate priorities.

One policy direction the incoming administration has already identified is a dedicated executive leadership position for tourism and destination development, separate from economic development. Calvo said they may be the first administration ever to dedicate an executive position to the industry of tourism.

“The position we’re looking at is actually tourism and destination development, separate from economic development, which is important,” Calvo said, “I think that would probably have fallen under economic development in the past, but we need to look at diversifying our economy and also protecting other growing industries separately.”

Ada said the position would reflect tourism’s significant impact on Guam’s economy and employment, particularly as the island’s tourism industry continues to face challenges.

When asked about their first 100 days in office, Ada said the administration will begin implementing its campaign plans after evaluating the government’s needs and establishing its leadership team. Calvo identified tourism, economic development, federal relations, and education as among the areas that will require attention.

When asked what the new administration is most excited to begin working on as they work toward a smooth government transition, they said they plan to continue monthly community cleanups, which began during the campaign.

“We want to still get out there and keep our community clean,” Ada said. “We want to ensure that, as we continue to move along within the first 100 days of our administration, that we start implementing our plans and get it to what we said during our campaign. You’re going to start seeing the implementation of those plans come to fruition.”

Ada and Calvo said they will seek guidance from former Republican governors and lieutenant governors to assist with the transition. Those invited to serve as honorary transition advisers include former governors Felix Camacho and Eddie Calvo, along with former lieutenant governors Ray Tenorio, Mike Cruz and Kaleo Moylan.

The transition team says additional appointments and opportunities for public participation will be announced in the coming weeks. Updates are expected through the incoming administration’s website and social media platforms.

item.title: CNMI runoff elections set for Nov. 20 after certification
item.description: The Commonwealth Election Commission is expected to certify the results of the 2026 general election Friday, formally triggering a 14-day countdown to runoff elections on Nov. 20 for governor and attorney general, according to CEC Executive Director Kayla Igitol Magofna. Magofna said Thursday that election commissioners are scheduled to certify the official results, setting into motion preparation
item.content:encoded:
The Commonwealth Election Commission is expected to certify the results of the 2026 general election Friday, formally triggering a 14-day countdown to runoff elections on Nov. 20 for governor and attorney general, according to CEC Executive Director Kayla Igitol Magofna.

Magofna said Thursday that election commissioners are scheduled to certify the official results, setting into motion preparations for the runoff election required under CNMI law when no candidate secures more than 50% of all votes cast and counted.

"So we have to have an election 14 days after," Magofna said.

The certification will finalize results from the Nov. 3 general election and establish the timeline for distributing runoff ballots and preparing polling sites across the Commonwealth.

According to the CEC, absentee voters who requested ballots for the general election will automatically receive absentee ballots for the runoff election. Election officials said no new requests for overseas absentee ballots will be accepted, although over-the-counter absentee voting will remain available.

Earlier, the commission mailed out 1,420 absentee ballots for the general election. Election officials counted 886 absentee ballots in the final tabulation and noted that ballots had to be received on Saipan on or before Election Day to be included in the certified results.

For the runoff election, the commission said it will continue to receive absentee ballots for up to 14 days after Election Day pursuant to its established procedures.

The certified results are expected to confirm runoff contests in both the governor's and attorney general's races.

In the gubernatorial contest, the Republican ticket of Ralph DLG Torres and Benjamin Jones Jr. led the field with 6,437 votes, or 49.5% of ballots cast, narrowly missing the majority needed to avoid a runoff. The independent ticket of Blas Jonathan Attao and Edmund Villagomez finished second with 5,043 votes, or 38.7%, advancing to the Nov. 20 runoff.

The independent team of Lawrence F. Camacho and Edith Deleon Guerrero placed third with 1,537 votes, or 11.8%.

The attorney general race also failed to produce a majority winner. Attorney Joaquin DLG Torres received 5,073 votes, or 39.7%, while attorney Michael Evangelista secured 3,854 votes, or 30.2%. Attorney Jonathan Robert Glass Jr. followed closely with 3,836 votes, or 30.1%.

Under CNMI law, the top two vote-getters advance to a runoff when no gubernatorial candidate or attorney general candidate receives more than half of all votes cast and counted.

The Commonwealth had 18,521 registered voters for the 2026 election. More than 13,000 voters cast ballots in the gubernatorial race, leaving roughly 5,500 registered voters who did not participate.

Election officials said registered voters who did not vote in the general election remain eligible to cast ballots in the Nov. 20 runoff election.

With certification anticipated Friday, election administrators will have two weeks to complete preparations for what is expected to be a closely watched runoff that will determine the Commonwealth's next governor and attorney general.

item.content:encoded:
The 39 th Guam Legislature will bring new faces, as well as some returning senators, into Guam’s lawmaking body.

A number of senators in the 38 th Guam Legislature gave up their seats to run for higher office. Republican Speaker Frank Blas Jr., Republican Vice Speaker Tony Ada and Democratic Sens. Therese Terlaje and Joe San Agustin all ran for governor, with Ada winning the island’s highest office.

Democratic Sens. Sabina Perez and Tina Muna Barnes ran for lieutenant governor.

That left nine incumbents, all of whom won reelection.

They are Republicans Sabrina Salas Matanane, Jesse Lujan, Chris Duenas, Shelly Calvo, Telo Taitague, Vincent Borja and Eulogio Shawn Gumatatao. Democratic incumbents reelected were Chris Barnett and William Parkinson.

Former Democratic Sens. Amanda Shelton, Telena Nelson and Clynton Ridgell were elected Tuesday, along with Democratic legislative newcomers Donna Quinata and Kallen Perez.

Hoa Nyugen is the Republican newcomer, giving the party an 8-7 majority in the 39 th Legislature.

item.title: Fears of an AI crackdown after midterms spark $2 trillion rout in tech stocks
item.description: Two days after Democrats won overwhelmingly in the national midterm elections — and in state races across the country — investors started to come to terms with the potential consequences. Fears that an incoming Democratic Congress would crack down on AI sent the tech-heavy Nasdaq down more than 5% and wiped out more than $2 trillion in market value. The Dow Jones and S&P also sank.
item.content:encoded:
Two days after Democrats won overwhelmingly in the national midterm elections — and in state races across the country — investors started to come to terms with the potential consequences.

Fears that an incoming Democratic Congress would crack down on AI sent the tech-heavy Nasdaq down more than 5% and wiped out more than $2 trillion in market value. The Dow Jones and S&P also sank.

The losses were a stark reversal from Wednesday, when investors had initially sent shares higher across the board, relieved that the midterms did not end with the fate of Congress undecided.

The sobering-up seen across markets on Thursday reflected investors' concern about a big signal sent by voters: They revolted against AI data centers , which many people worry will gobble up water and energy resources. Those voters supported Democrats who have vowed to push back against the proliferation of these projects.

But many AI companies — including Meta and Alphabet, the parent company of Google — need to keep building out these data centers to continue developing the technology.

The Nasdaq's decline comes after what has already been a rough year of technology shares on Wall Street, with investors starting to question whether the massive investments companies have plowed into AI will pay off anytime soon.

"There is some concern regarding AI regulation, and fears that there could be far more regulations coming to AI technology, as well as a pushback on the buildout of data centers across the country," says David Busch, chief investment officer of Trajan Wealth.

AI-related or AI-dependent stocks of all kinds were among the biggest decliners on Thursday, with Tesla and SpaceX — both controlled by billionaire Elon Musk — falling particularly sharply. Musk spent hundreds of millions of dollars in an unsuccessful attempt to elect more Republicans, and investors fear he and his companies could also come under Democratic scrutiny when the new Congress is seated in January.

It's not only Congress, however. Democrats who vowed to slow down AI development also won at the state level, most prominently Gina Hinojosa, who won the Texas governor's race in stunning fashion.

It's unclear whether the AI stock rout will continue — or spread beyond tech stocks. AI has become a big driver of the U.S. economy, helping it post a solid annual growth of 3.4% in the July-September quarter.

And sophisticated Wall Street investors are not the only ones who own a lot of shares in AI companies. Average Americans also own them through their retirement investment portfolios — such as 401(k)s or pension funds — leaving them also vulnerable to a prolonged AI rout.

item.content:encoded:
Democrats are poised to have a strong majority in the upcoming Congress. The final numbers are still being determined and several races are still outstanding.

A few in California are being contested by two candidates in the same party. So it's clear which party will hold the seat, even if it's not clear who will win. Others are too close to call or there aren't enough ballots counted to know which candidate will prevail. In many places in the country, it takes a while to count votes . That's normal and expected.

Here's where things stand in the races that are waiting to be called in the House by The Associated Press:

In the Senate, there are two races outstanding, Alaska and Mississippi. Because Alaska uses ranked choice voting and no candidate in the four-person race has achieved a 50% majority in the count, it may proceed to another round of counting later this month. Mississippi uses a more traditional electoral system but a large number of provisional ballots — called affidavit ballots in the state — are taking time to count. Less than 2,000 votes separate the top two candidates in that race.

item.title: Melania Trump touts rare agreement she brokered between Russia and Ukraine
item.description: First lady Melania Trump hosted a rare meeting between Russian and Ukrainian officials at the White House to recognize a temporary ceasefire in southeastern Ukraine . The six-day pause from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky comes as the administration ramps up efforts to secure an agreement to end the war in Ukraine.
item.content:encoded:
First lady Melania Trump hosted a rare meeting between Russian and Ukrainian officials at the White House to recognize a temporary ceasefire in southeastern Ukraine .

The six-day pause from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky comes as the administration ramps up efforts to secure an agreement to end the war in Ukraine.

"We have chosen humanity over war," the first lady said. "Undeniably, the lives of innocent people must transcend the divisions of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace."

Trump has accomplished something that has so far eluded her husband - helping broker a temporary ceasefire and bringing together representatives of the two sides in acknowledgement of the human costs of the war.

The White House sees it as a diplomatic breakthrough, but some European analysts worry the efforts can backfire.

The temporary reprieve, which expired on Sunday, enabled humanitarian aid to reach the city while allowing hundreds of residents to be evacuated.

Kirill Dmitriev, Russian President Vladimir Putin's special envoy, thanked the first lady. He said Putin personally gave the instructions to ensure the successful implementation of the ceasefire.

"On behalf of President Putin, on behalf of the people of the Russian Federation, we would like to thank first lady Melania Trump for her distinguished humanitarian role in resolving a key situation and resolving this humanitarian issue," he said.

Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets presented Melania Trump with an award for her humanitarian work. The Order of Princess Olha, 1st Class, is Ukraine's highest award for women.

"I have only one request from all Ukrainian nation," Lubinets said, "please continue doing your wonderful work and support people."

The event comes just days before the U.S. leads a new round of peace talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi next week.

President Trump also met with Dmitriev at the White House.

Trump told reporters that the sides were close to reaching a deal.

"It's going to be an agreement. It's going to be a big agreement, ‌and ⁠it's going to involve more than Ukraine," he said. "I could even say it might involve all of Europe. It's ⁠going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone's going to be thrilled."

Heather Conley, who worked on European issues in President George W. Bush's State Department, supports all efforts to help suffering Ukrainians, but she also said the U.S. must be careful not to normalize Russia's bad behavior.

"In this White House ceremony, we were honoring the Russians that were the cause of both the occupation of Oleshky, the starvation of Oleshky, and now we're honoring them for allowing aid to come into Oleshky," said Conley, who is now a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. "The more we create this equivalency where the Russians and the Ukrainians are equal in this crisis, it is putting this thing upside down."

item.title: How North Carolina Democrats flipped several House seats in historically GOP districts
item.description: The Associated Press has called five U.S. House races in North Carolina for Democrats, all of them in districts drawn to favor Republican candidates. Of those districts, four are flipping from Republican control.
item.content:encoded:
The Associated Press has called five U.S. House races in North Carolina for Democrats, all of them in districts drawn to favor Republican candidates.

Of those districts, four are flipping from Republican control.

As of Thursday, the AP had called nine of the state's 14 House seats for Democrats and none for Republicans. It's a startling result for a delegation that went into Tuesday with 10 Republicans and four Democrats.

Races called Thursday that flipped from Republican to Democratic control included:

North Carolina's Congressional map was redrawn in 2023 to significantly favor Republican candidates, and these four districts performed that way in 2024. The 14th District was the closest in that election, with Moore winning by about 16%, while the 6th District was the least competitive, with McDowell winning by more than 38%.

One of the candidates vying to replace Hudson as NRCC chair is U.S. Rep. Brian Jack, a Georgia Republican.

He wrote in a letter to fellow House Republicans that fellow GOP lawmakers may have contributed to the challenging environment. Former Gov. Roy Cooper, a Democrat, won the race for North Carolina's open U.S. Senate seat by nearly 20%.

"When Senate Republicans withdrew support from North Carolina weeks ago, they created a cascade that likely swept away many of our colleagues from that state," Jack wrote.

The AP also called northeastern North Carolina's 1st Congressional District for incumbent Democrat Rep. Don Davis on Thursday.

That's a district legislative Republicans redrew last year in an effort to make it easier for GOP candidates to win there, pulling Republican-leaning counties from the state's 3rd Congressional District to do so.

Yet as of Thursday, Davis was leading Republican challenger Laurie Buckhout by more than 10,000 votes. That's a larger margin than he won by in 2024.

North Carolina's 3rd Congressional District is one of five in the state that remain uncalled, with incumbent Republican Greg Murphy leading Democrat Raymond Smith by just 233 votes in a district where Democrats didn't even run a candidate in 2024. That race is likely headed for a recount.

In the 5th Congressional District, Democratic challenger Chuck Hubbard is leading 11-term Republican incumbent Virginia Foxx by 99 votes — that's another race that may go to a recount.

If all of the remaining results hold, the state's congressional delegation would flip from 10 Republicans and four Democrats to 10 Democrats and four Republicans.
